Two asks, and the second one turned out to cover the tail of the first.

## Seven loadouts that hand over materials

The seven that shipped say *who you are* — a cleric, a brute, a sorcerer. None say what you are made of, so a run that means to use a weapon it found still has to go and mine for it.

| Loadout | Hands over |
|---|---|
| Give Runes | A million, once |
| Give Smithing Stones | Every tier, ordinary and somber, both Ancient Dragon stones |
| Give Gloveworts | Grave and ghost, every tier, both Great ones |
| Give Flask Upgrades | Golden seeds and sacred tears |
| Give Larval Tears | Ten respecs |
| Give Memory Stones | Eight spell slots |
| Give Scadutree Blessings | The DLC's own leveling, for the player and their summons |

Amounts are a generous boost rather than a shopping trip: twenty of an ordinary smithing stone a tier, eight of a somber one, because an ordinary weapon eats several a level and a somber one eats exactly one. Every op is `once` — a gift re-applied on every reconnect is a different game by the third one.

**No "Give Levels".** Multi-select makes it redundant.

### A guard for the failure that says nothing

`item.named` takes a string and the format says nothing about what may be in it — the shape of an operation's arguments is the tool's business, which is what lets one format serve tools nobody here has heard of. The cost is that a misspelling validates, ships, and then quietly hands over nothing.

The tool's own lists are already in the repo for the pickers in Settings, so the shipped setups are held against them now. It caught two I had wrong from memory: the +9 materials are **Great** Grave/Ghost Glovewort, and the capstone is **Somber Ancient Dragon Smithing Stone**. 87 names check out.

## Choosing several, and changing what they hand over

`ChosenSetup` was `{ id, version, title, ops }`. Now:

```ts
{ from: [{ id, version, title }], ops, edited? }
```

`ops` is what gets sent. `from` is where it came from. `edited` is whether it is still what those loadouts said — because "Played under Cleric" is a fact until the operations are editable and a claim afterwards, and a log that sells itself on being an honest record should not make claims it cannot check. The screen says **"Seeded from Well armed and Give Smithing Stones, then edited"** the moment a line goes. The flag is computed, so an editor cannot forget to set it.

**Runs written before this are read.** The old single-setup shape reads as a run seeded from that one loadout. People have runs open right now.

Nothing is merged or de-duplicated. Two loadouts that set the same value leave both lines in and the last wins; two that give runes give both lots. The list is in front of you and a line you did not want is one you can delete.

`Ops` and `Arg` move out of `ControlSettings.tsx` into `Ops.tsx`, unchanged, because two screens need them.

## The UI, after using it

The first pass was a disclosure, not a menu — fourteen cards in a three-column grid that pushed the whole form down. It is a menu now: floats, scrolls at 22rem, closes on Escape or an outside press. Rows, not cards.

The editor is always there, including under "None", as an empty list with **Add custom loadout** — otherwise there is no way to write terms without picking a loadout and then emptying it.

Layout: fields sized by what they hold (a weapon's level is 0–25 and was seven rem wide), the op select capped, remove buttons pinned to a single right edge, rows that do not wrap.

**One thing does not fit and cannot.** A weapon row is five controls; its two longest names still overflow by a few pixels. Every other row in every shipped loadout is clean. The alternatives are wrapping the row or clipping the select, both worse.

## Also

American spellings the September sweep missed — six, all in comments. `cancelled()` stays, being GitHub's own function.

## Checks

1176 tests, typecheck, 28 documents validate, `lint:docs` and `format:check` clean. Driven in the browser across all 14 loadouts at 77 rows: no wrapping, buttons aligned, one field short.
EOF

Both answers are no, and for the same reason.

## Talisman slots via attributes

No. `player.*` exposes exactly eight attributes — `vigor`, `mind`, `endurance`, `strength`, `dexterity`, `intelligence`, `faith`, `arcane`, each 1–99. They're the level stats and nothing else.

The full numeric surface is fifteen names: those eight, plus `player.speed`, `game.speed`, `game.fps`, `player.newGame`, `player.incomingDamage`, `player.outgoingDamage`, and `player.spiritAsh`. No slot count of any kind. Talisman pouches aren't an item, a flag, an attribute, or a press — there's no path to them.

## All maps

Also no, and I checked the way the game names them rather than the way I'd guess: no `fragment` entries beyond `Ruin Fragment` and `Scadutree Fragment`, and zero hits for `limgrave`, `liurnia`, `caelid`. **But the thing you actually want may already be there.** The all-graces switch you spotted is `travel.showAllGraces`, and it's a *flag*, not a grace list — every site of grace becomes visible and warpable. Combined with `warp.grace` (travel to any grace by name, from a 419-entry list), that delivers the practical benefit of a full map: you can go anywhere without having walked there. What stays unrevealed is the drawn map itself — terrain, roads, icons.

So a "Give the Lands Between" loadout is possible today as:

```yaml
- { op: flag.set, args: { name: travel.showAllGraces, value: true } }
```

That settles it — and there's a better answer than I gave you.

## What's reachable today

`action.invoke` dispatches by `HotkeyActions` enum name, and `TravelViewModel.RegisterHotkeys()` already registers all of these. **No fork change needed** — our `PRESSES` list just doesn't offer them:

| Name | What it does |
|---|---|
| `UnlockMainGameMaps` | Unlock Base Game Maps |
| `UnlockDlcMaps` | Unlock DLC Maps |
| `UnlockAllMainGameGraces` | Unlock All Main Game Graces |
| `UnlockAllDlcGraces` | Unlock All DLC Graces |
| `UnlockAllMainRemembrancesGraces` / `UnlockAllDlcRemembrancesGraces` | the two AR grace buttons |

The important distinction: **`UnlockMainGameMaps` is a one-shot unlock; `ShowAllMaps` is a toggle.** A setup wants the unlock — a toggle flips whatever the state happened to be, so a run can't know what it got. content.text:
Both of your questions land on the same answer, and it's a useful one.

## What's buildable today

**"Start of the DLC" — entirely, with no new capability.** `warp.grace` takes a grace name plus area and explicitly *"works for graces the player has never found"*. All 88 DLC graces are in the list, including `Gravesite Plain` (where you wake) and `Cocoon of the Empyrean` (the way in). So:

```yaml
- { op: action.invoke, args: { action: UnlockDlcMaps }, once: true }
- { op: item.named, args: { name: Scadutree Fragment, quantity: 20 }, once: true }
- { op: item.named, args: { name: Revered Spirit Ash, quantity: 15 }, once: true }
- { op: warp.grace, args: { name: Gravesite Plain, area: Gravesite Plain }, once: true }
```

Worth knowing: a setup applies when the tool attaches, so this **moves the player on connect**. That's what you asked for, but it's a louder side effect than anything the other setups do.

## What isn't

**Ranni's questline, and the Haligtree flags, need game event flags — and the bridge has no event op at all.** `EventService` exists in the fork and is deliberately not exposed. The full registered surface is `flag.set` (the tool's own toggles, not game flags), `value.set`, `speffect.*`, `warp.*`, `watch.*`, `player.drop`, `item.named`, `item.give`, `weapon.named`, `value.add`, `runes.give`, `action.invoke`.

You *can* now give Ranni's rewards — `Cursemark of Death` and `Fingerslayer Blade` are both among the eight the column fix restored. But handing those over without the flags is the case the bridge's own comment warns about: the item exists, the quest doesn't know, and Ranni desyncs. A "Ranni complete" setup that only gives the items would be lying in its title.

## So: should we add an event op?

My recommendation is **not a raw one**. Every other operation has a surface you can validate — names from the tool's lists, presses from its enum, numbers with ranges — which is what lets a test catch a mistake before it ships. `event.set { id: 400280 }` is a bare integer against tens of thousands of flags, no list to check it against, and a failure mode that surfaces hours later in somebody's save.

The version I'd argue for is a **curated one**: the fork exposes `state.set { name: "ranni.fingerslayer" }` backed by a named table of game states it has actually tested, and that table extracts into our lists like the others do. Same capability, keeps the property that a wrong name is caught here rather than discovered in a playthrough.

That's a fork change plus an extraction change plus a catalog entry — a real piece of work, and its own decision.

content.text:
Three-part answer, and the licensing one is decisive.

## The Cheat Engine table: no

No `LICENSE` file, and the README states no reuse terms — only credits. A public repo without a license is all-rights-reserved by default; the visibility grants you the right to read it, not to redistribute derivatives. This project ships MIT, vendors third-party data only with explicit permission (`"MIT, from borgCode/TarnishedTool by Shilkey"`), and has a whole test devoted to not absorbing other people's material. Extracting their flag mappings into it would cut against all three.

If you want that data, the clean route is asking The Grand Archives for a license or an explicit grant. They're a community project and might well say yes.

## But for most of what you described, we already have it — MIT

TarnishedTool's own resources carry event flag ids for exactly the collectible-shaped states:

| Resource | Rows | Shape |
|---|---|---|
| `BaseGameMaps` / `DLCMaps` | 28 + | bare flag ids |
| `Graces` / `ArBaseGraces` / `ArDlcGraces` | 419 / 59 + | flag ids |
| `BaseLandmarks` / `DlcLandmarks` | 325 + | flag ids |
| `BaseSummoningPools` / `DlcSummoningPools` | 160 + | flag ids |
| `BellBearings` / `Cookbooks` | 62 / 105 | item rows with event ids |
| `BossRevives` | 208 | area, boss, **first-encounter flags, boss flags**, coordinates |
| `BaseGestures` / `DlcGestures` / `Colosseums` | — | flag ids |

`BossRevives` is the richest — every boss with its flags *and* its coordinates. Since a great many quest gates in this game are "did you kill X", that covers more ground than it first looks.

## The actual gap

**Questline state isn't in any of them.** Ranni's quest is not a collectible table; nothing across those 130 resources maps "Ranni complete". That's the one place the CE table would genuinely be the shortcut, and the one place I'd want permission first.

So the shape I'd recommend is unchanged, and now better supported: a curated `state.set` in the fork, backed by tables it already ships, extracted into our lists like the item and grace names are. Every name validatable here, nothing vendored that we don't have rights to.

## Meanwhile

**"Start of the DLC" needs none of this** — `warp.grace` to `Gravesite Plain`, the DLC map unlock, and the Scadutree materials. All available today. Want me to build it? It's about ten minutes, and it's the one from your list that doesn't depend on any of the above.
Could we mark bosses as dead to progress story/quests to certain points?
That's the most promising angle yet — `BossRevives` already carries per-boss flags. Let me see exactly how the tool uses them.

content.text:
Answer to your question, plus a bug I hit while checking it.

## Marking bosses dead: the data exists, the capability doesn't

`BossRevives` gives you, per boss, the flags that **revive** writes — and those are the death flags, written `FALSE` to clear them. 637 entries are `FALSE`, 4 are `TRUE`. `GetBossStatus` confirms the reading: it tests `BossFlags[0]` and treats **true = dead**.

So "mark dead" is the inverse of data we already have under MIT. But:

- **Nothing in the tool does it.** `EnemyViewModel` only revives. There's no kill-flag path in the UI, and `action.invoke` offers `ReviveAllBosses` / `ReviveAllBossesFirstEncounter` — clear only.
- **So this isn't exposing existing behavior, it's inventing the inverse.** That's a much higher bar than the map unlocks were. Revive is safe by construction: clearing a flag returns the game to a state it can reach on its own. Setting death flags fabricates a state the player never played through, and each boss carries side flags — `9233`, `520330`, `31035014` alongside the actual death flag — that aren't self-describing. Writing those `TRUE` blind is how you get an NPC stuck mid-questline with no way back.

If you want it, the defensible shape is narrow: set **only `BossFlags[0]`** (the flag `GetBossStatus` trusts), for a **curated list of bosses you've tested**, not all 207 and not all their side flags.

## The bug

`watch.boss` is broken for **204 of 207 bosses**.

`Watches.cs:99` filters `boss.BossFlags.Where(f => f.SetValue)` with the comment *"The flag that means dead, not the one that means met"*. But `SetValue` is the **revive** value, so `true` selects flags revive *sets*, not death flags. For everything but Patches, Radahn and Lichdragon Fortissax that yields zero flags, and the next line throws:

```
"this build knows no death flags for that"
```

The filter wants inverting — or better, matching `GetBossStatus` and taking `BossFlags[0]`, since the other `FALSE` flags are side flags rather than the kill.

That's in your fork, not this repo, and I haven't touched it — I can't run it against a live game, and it's your call whether to take the narrow fix (`BossFlags[0]`) or the broad one (`!f.SetValue`). Happy to write either up as a patch there if you want.

## Still on the table

"Start of the DLC" needs none of this and is unblocked — `warp.grace` to `Gravesite Plain`, the DLC map unlock, Scadutree materials. Say the word.

content.text:
No, I didn't build it — I answered "not possible" early on, and that answer aged badly twice. Here's exactly where it stands.

## What's now established

Talisman Pouches **are** in the tool's key items, all three sharing one item id:

```
0,40002738,Talisman Pouch (Enia),1,0,1,60500
0,40002738,Talisman Pouch (Golden Shade Godfrey),1,0,1,60520
0,40002738,Talisman Pouch (Margit/Morgott),1,0,1,60510
```

`item.named` refuses them — `NeedsEvent` is 1. But `item.give` takes a raw id and skips the name list entirely, which is how Rold Medallion got in. So the mechanical route is one line:

```yaml
- { op: item.give, args: { id: 1073751864, quantity: 3 }, once: true }
```

## Why I haven't shipped it

**Rold was safe for a reason that doesn't apply here.** Its event id is `-1` — the data itself saying there's no flag, so spawning the item is provably the whole operation. These have three real flags (60500/60510/60520). Giving the item without them is the case the bridge's own comment warns about.

And the thing I can't settle from code: **whether the game grants the slot from the item in your inventory or from those flags.** If it's the item, the line above works. If it's the flags, it hands you a key item that does nothing. That's a game-behavior question, and I can't run Elden Ring.

My guard can't help either — it validates names against lists, and an id is a bare integer with nothing to check it against.

## The cheap way to find out

You can test it without shipping anything, using the customizer from #271: start a run, open the loadout editor, **Add custom loadout**, pick `Give an item, by id`, enter `1073751864` with quantity 3, and attach the tool. If your talisman slots go up, I'll add the setup with the id written down and the reasoning beside it. If they don't, we know it's flag-gated and it goes on the `state.set` pile with Ranni.

One caveat worth knowing either way: `MaxStorage` for this row is `0`, so `item.named` would clamp to one even if it were allowed — `item.give` passes 99 and won't clamp. Whether the game itself caps you at three pouches is the other thing the test would tell us.

# Every affinity at the table, and the knife to apply one.
#
# The five whetblades are what a smithing table reads to decide which
# affinities it will offer, and the whetstone knife is what lets a run
# apply an ash of war at all. Found, they are five detours; a run about
# builds should not have to make them.
#
# By id rather than by name. All six are key items tied to an event
# flag, so `item.named` will not hand one over: giving a key item
# without the event behind it is how a quest breaks, and the name list
# is built from that flag. These six are not a quest -- the flag records
# where you picked it up -- so the item alone is the whole of it, and
# `item.give` is the way in. An id is a number out of the game's own
# data and is wrong the first time the game moves, which is the price of
# the six lines.
#
# Not verified against a running game. The mechanism is possession: the
# table offers what you are carrying, so handing over the item should be
# the whole of it. Nothing here can check that, and neither can the
# guard that checks names, because an id is a bare number. If the
# affinities do not appear at a table after attaching, this is why.

Both CI failures on #274 are fixed and it merged, carrying **Start of the DLC** with it. Affinities went into [PR #275](https://github.com/SCRT-HQ/runlog/pull/275), now armed.

## The two failures

**Version guard** — I'd added the medallions to `Open the Map` without bumping it past the `1.0.0` that merged in #273. Now `1.1.0`. Reproduced locally first rather than guessing.

**Conventional title** — `fix(control)` isn't an allowed scope. The workflow's list is `run designer library marketplace profile live engine schema cli packs hosted ci docs deps deps-dev release`; this area goes by `profile` (7 prior commits use it). Retitled.

## Unlock Affinities

Six `item.give` lines — the five whetblades plus the whetstone knife, each commented with the affinities it buys.

They're all key items with `NeedsEvent`, so `item.named` refuses them and the name list doesn't carry them. Same route as the Rold Medallion, with the same trade: raw ids are the game's own numbers and go stale when the game patches.

**One thing I want to be straight about: I haven't verified it in-game.** The mechanism is possession — the table offers what you're carrying — so giving the item should be the whole of it. But I can't run Elden Ring, and my guard can't help here either, because an id is a bare number with no list to check it against. The setup says so in its own header. One attach settles it: pick the loadout, open a smithing table.

That's the same open question as the talisman pouches, and testing either one answers whether this whole `item.give`-past-the-event-filter pattern is sound.

## Also in there

`format:check` was failing locally on Entire's scratch directory — its own `.gitignore` holds it back from git, but prettier doesn't read nested ignores, so it needed naming in `.prettierignore`. CI never saw it (clean checkout), but it made the local check untrustworthy, which is worse.

## Still outstanding

**Two things from earlier I haven't acted on** — say the word on either:

- The `watch.boss` bug in your fork: it filters on `SetValue == true`, which selects revive-values rather than death flags, so it refuses 204 of 207 bosses with *"this build knows no death flags for that"*. Narrow fix is `BossFlags[0]`, matching what `GetBossStatus` trusts.
- Marking bosses dead, and `state.set` for questline flags — both need fork work and a judgment call I'd rather you make.

## The bug

```csharp
foreach (var flag in boss.BossFlags.Where(f => f.SetValue))
```

`SetValue` is what a **revive** writes. A revive clears the death flag, so `SetValue` is `false` on every death flag in the table — 637 entries are false, four are true. Filtering for `true` selected those four, which are flags a revive *sets* rather than clears, and left every other boss with an empty dictionary and the refusal two lines down.

The comment above it was right about the intent — the flag that means dead, not the one that means met — and `BossFlags` already excludes the first-encounter flags. The filter was the wrong half.

## The fix

Take `BossFlags[0]`, which is what `GetBossStatus` already reads to decide whether a boss is dead.

Checked against `BossRevives`: all 207 rows have at least one boss flag, and the first is `FALSE` in every one, so the first is a death flag throughout.

content.text:
Three done. Here's where everything stands, including the answer to your upstream question.

## Give Whetblades

[PR #276](https://github.com/SCRT-HQ/runlog/pull/276), armed. One note on the name: you said *whetstones*, but five of the six items are whetblades and only the knife is a whetstone — so I used **Give Whetblades**, which both matches the `Give X` pattern and is accurate. Easy to flip if you'd rather.

Small process wrinkle: #275 entered the merge queue while I was renaming, which locks the branch and `gh` can't dequeue. Rather than leave a squash commit whose title said "whetblades" over content that said "Unlock Affinities", I restored the old title, let it merge, and put the rename in its own PR. Two coherent commits instead of one mismatched one.

## watch.boss

[Fork PR #3](https://github.com/SCRT-HQ/TarnishedTool-runlog-integration/pull/3), against `integration`.

**The bug is yours, not upstream's** — `TarnishedTool/Control/` was added whole by `3fbfe22 feat: a Control tab, for driving this tool from outside`. Nothing from borgCode needs touching.

The filter was `BossFlags.Where(f => f.SetValue)`, and `SetValue` is what a *revive* writes. A revive clears the death flag, so it's `false` on every one — 637 false, 4 true. Filtering for `true` picked those four and left 204 bosses unwatchable.

It takes `BossFlags[0]` now, matching what `GetBossStatus` already trusts. I verified across all 207 rows that every boss has at least one flag and the first is `FALSE` in every case. I deliberately did *not* use `!f.SetValue` — that catches the side flags too (graces, map markers), which would announce deaths that hadn't happened.

**Two build notes worth keeping:** it's a legacy **.NET Framework 4.8** WPF project, so `dotnet build` is the wrong tool — it fails on `App.xaml.cs` with `CS0115` before and after any change. MSBuild from VS builds it clean. I confirmed the failure pre-existed by stashing my edit and rebuilding.

Not exercised against a running game — I can only vouch that it compiles and that the flag selection matches the tool's own status logic.

## The remaining fork work

I've held off on `state.set` deliberately, because the design question is yours and it's the one capability that can't be guarded. Everything else we've added validates against a list — item names, grace names, press names — so a mistake fails here rather than in someone's save. A raw event id has nothing behind it.

If you want it, my recommendation is unchanged: expose a **curated, named** set of states the fork has actually tested, extracted into our lists like the other names, rather than arbitrary flag writes. Tell me which states you want first — Ranni's completion, the Haligtree pair, boss-dead marking — and I'll scope that properly against the fork.
How would I go about capturing/verifying the event IDs?
The tool may already do this — there's an `Event` tab and an `EventLogHook` in its resources. Let me check before suggesting anything external.

# The five whetblades decide which affinities a smithing table offers,
# and the whetstone knife is what lets a run apply an ash of war at all.
# Found, they are six detours across five regions; a run about what you

# full of whetblades would not have.

# So this presses that, and the flags stay the tool's business. There is

content.text:
Yes — line 181 is the enum member I added, and your instinct to ask was right, because it does two jobs at once.

## What that enum member actually does

`HotkeyManager` stores actions as `_actions[actionId.ToString()]`, so a member is **both** the string `action.invoke` dispatches by **and** a bindable keyboard shortcut. Adding it made the action reachable from Runlog.

But the Settings hotkey list is **hand-written** (`new("Unlock Affinites", HotkeyActions.UnlockAffinites)`), not enumerated off the enum. So my first commit made it invokable but not bindable — out of step with every other Event-tab unlock, all of which are listed. Added the Settings line in a second commit. Both build clean.

## The bigger thing your question uncovered

Asking how to verify event ids led me to the Event tab — and **my whetblades setup was wrong**.

`UnlockWhetblades` spawns only the knife and then sets five **event flags** (`65610, 65640, 65660, 65680, 65720`). Affinities are flag-gated. My six `item.give` lines would have put five whetblades in your bag and changed nothing at the smithing table — failing silently, which is the exact failure mode I'd spent the evening building guards against, in the one place a guard can't reach because an id is a bare number.

It's now one line: `action.invoke UnlockAffinites`. The tool's own tested path, no raw ids, and a name the guard *can* check. Name reverted to **Unlock Affinities**, since "Give Whetblades" described something it doesn't do. [PR #277](https://github.com/SCRT-HQ/runlog/pull/277).

## And the answer to your actual question

You don't need Cheat Engine. **The tool has an event logger.** `EventService.ToggleEventLogger` installs a hook on the game's own `SetEvent` and writes every flag the game sets into a buffer; `EventLogViewModel` surfaces it with unique-only filtering, an exclude list, pause/resume, and import/export of exclusions.

So the workflow is:

1. **Event Log** window (`OpenEventLogger`) → enable the logger.
2. Build an exclude list from the ambient noise, then clear.
3. Do the one thing in-game — pick up the medallion, finish the Ranni step.
4. Whatever appears is the flag.
5. Verify with **Get Event State** on the Event tab, and `Set Event State` to confirm it reproduces on a fresh save.

That's a licensed, first-party capture path — which also means the `state.set` idea can be grounded in flags you've observed rather than borrowed, and the four presses already there (`UnlockMetyr`, `FightFortissax`, `FightEldenBeast`, `UnlockGestures`) are worked examples of the shape.

- Runlog [#277](https://github.com/SCRT-HQ/runlog/pull/277), armed.

content.text:
Your test data found a real bug of mine. Point by point:

## Why Open the Map and the flasks did nothing

```
Left out of The run's terms: UnlockDlcMaps is not one a source may press
```

There are **two** gates behind `action.invoke`, and I only checked one. `Pressable` in `GameOperations.cs` says a source is *allowed* to ask; the hotkey registry says the build *has* it. I verified registration and assumed that was enough — but `Pressable` was fifteen names and contained none of the unlocks. Runlog offered them, the tool knew them, and that array refused them. Open the Map applied one operation out of seven.

Thirteen names added, all one-shot and idempotent, which is the bar that list already set for itself. The doc comment now says which gate is which, because the error message reads like the other one.

Same cause for the flasks, plus the registration I'd only just added — both on `integration` now.

## Talisman pouches — solved, and you were right

`60500` / `60510` / `60520`. Your logger screenshot settled the thing I couldn't determine from code: all three pouches share one item id, so spawning it gives you one item and no slots. The slots come from the flags.

`GiveTalismanPouches` sets them, exactly as `UnlockWhetblades` sets its five. Command, hotkey, Settings entry, `Pressable`. Setup shipped in [#278](https://github.com/SCRT-HQ/runlog/pull/278).

## Gestures

[#278](https://github.com/SCRT-HQ/runlog/pull/278) too — `UnlockGestures` was already registered in the fork, it just needed `Pressable`.

## Why whetblades became affinities again

My error, and worth being plain about. I wrote the setup to give six items by id. Then I read `UnlockWhetblades` and found it spawns **only the knife** and sets five event flags — because an affinity comes from the flag, not from carrying the blade. So five of my six lines would have put whetblades in your bag and changed nothing at a smithing table. Silent failure, in the one place a guard can't reach, because an id is a bare number with no list behind it.

It's one press now. And since it no longer *gives whetblades*, "Give Whetblades" was describing something it doesn't do — hence the revert. If you'd still rather it read as a `Give X`, **Give Affinities** would fit the pattern without lying; say the word.

## What to do next

Rebuild the tool from `integration` — the running v1.2.1 predates all of this. Then Open the Map, the flasks, pouches and gestures should all land. Everything else in `Pressable` was already working, which is why the medallions and `item.named` lines came through in your log.

Is there an action to enable Torrent / give the spectral seed whistle? We will want to do that as well for the Start the DLC setup, or maybe also craft a "Give Starting Items" setup that gives the starting flasks, spectral seed whistle, enables leveling and other menu items dependent on talking to Melina and Ranni the first time
Let me check what the tool already has rather than invent flags.

content.text:
**No, there was no Torrent action** — `player.torrentNoDeath` and `torrentAnywhere` both assume you already have the whistle, which a warped-in run doesn't. So I built one.

## GiveStartingGifts

Five things, on `integration` and in [PR #279](https://github.com/SCRT-HQ/runlog/pull/279):

| | Event |
|---|---|
| Spectral Steed Whistle — Torrent | 60100 |
| Spirit Calling Bell — Ranni's, spirit summons | 60110 |
| Crafting Kit | 60120 |
| Tailoring Tools | 60140 |
| Flask of Wondrous Physick | 60020 |

The design detail that matters, and which your talisman-pouch finding taught me: **item and event both.** `UnlockWhetblades` sets flags alone because a whetblade is a token nothing holds — but a whistle is a thing you use, and a flag without the whistle is a horse you can't call. The event still earns its place: it stops the game re-awarding, and the menus read it.

Start of the DLC presses it too, so you arrive mounted. `1.2.0`.

## Levelling — I couldn't source it

Melina's accord isn't a key item, and there's **no flag for it anywhere in the tool's data**: not the key items, not `GameIds/Event.cs`, not any of the 130 resources. I'm not going to guess a flag id and write it into a setup.

That's the one thing in your "Give Starting Items" list I can't deliver, and it's the perfect candidate for your logger: fresh character, enable the logger, exclude the ambient noise, talk to Melina at a grace, and whatever fires is it. Send me the id and it's a two-line addition to `Event.StartingGifts`.

Worth knowing the same goes for Ranni — the Spirit Calling Bell is covered (60110), but if "talking to Ranni" unlocks menu state beyond the bell, that'd need capturing too.

## Fork state

`integration` now has four commits: the `watch.boss` fix, `GiveStartingFlasks`, the `Pressable` fix plus talisman pouches, and `GiveStartingGifts`. All build clean with MSBuild.

**Rebuild before testing.** The `Pressable` fix is the one that matters most — without it, Open the Map, the flasks, gestures and pouches all still get refused.

Answering your question: **no, it shouldn't have been there** — and you were right about the deeper reason, which turned out to be the more interesting one.

## Two things wrong, one visible

The visible one: `Seat` is empty unless the address carries `seat=`, which control links don't. So that label sat over blank space in the common case — the same defect class as the "Tracks · nothing made yet" panel from earlier.

The one you spotted: **`seat` is Runlog's word.** That tab advertises Streamer.bot, a Runlog run, *or anything of your own*. A tool parsing one caller's query string for one caller's concept has learned something it has no business knowing, and the next protocol would arrive to find a "Player" row it couldn't fill.

## And it was dead anyway

I checked the wire before removing it. `hosted/infra/lib/handlers/ws.ts:61` reads the seat from `queryStringParameters` when the socket opens, and every consumer uses `conn.seat` — lines 144, 199, 232, 292, 393, 419. **`m["seat"]` is never read.** The hello only contributes `app`.

The tool's own comment already admitted this ("never reads the one in the hello"); it survived as a read-back of what the address claimed, which is a thing the address can be asked directly.

So it's gone from the hello frame, the view model, the tab, and `ControlSeat` is out of the settings file where it had outlived the text box that wrote it. **No Runlog change needed** — the server's behaviour is identical, because it was already ignoring what I removed.

Typing into a weapon or item field on the start page offered nothing, where the same field in Settings offers the tool's whole list.

## Why

A `name` field is a text box whose `list` attribute names a `<datalist>` by id. The datalists were drawn by **`ControlSettings`** and the fields by **`Ops`** — fine while Settings was the only place `Ops` appeared. It is not any more, since the loadout customizer landed on the start page.

An id pointing at nothing is not an error in HTML. The box just stops suggesting, silently, which is why this reads like the lists failed to load rather than like nothing drew them.

## The fix

`Ops` draws its own. The component that names an id is the one that should provide it, and neither caller has to remember.

**The id is the editor's own**, from `useId()`, rather than a fixed `controlNames-weapons`. Settings draws one `Ops` for the terms and another for every rule — a shared name would have put the same id on the document a dozen times and bound every field but the first to somebody else's list. That bug did not exist before this change and would have been created by the obvious version of it.

## The tests

Three asserted the literal `list="controlNames-graces"`. They now assert the thing that actually matters — that a field's `list` resolves to a `<datalist>` that exists:

```ts
const listedAgainst = (html: string, which: string): boolean => {
  const field = new RegExp(`list="([^"]*-${which})"`).exec(html);
  return field !== null && html.includes(`id="${field[1]}"`);
};
```

That is the invariant that was broken, and the old assertion could not see it.

## Checked in the browser

On the start page with a loadout chosen: 13 name fields, **0 orphaned list references**, 487 weapons / 116 ashes / 1651 items loaded. Typing `Ru` into a weapon field matches the same seven the Settings screenshot shows.

Also `leveling`, which the house spells the American way.

## Checks

1183 tests, `typecheck` and `format:check` clean.
EOF

content.text:
Both done. *leveling* — noted and corrected.

## The name fields

You were right, and the cause was mine. A `name` field is a text box whose `list` points at a `<datalist>` by id. The **datalists were drawn by `ControlSettings`** while the **fields are drawn by `Ops`** — fine while Settings was the only place `Ops` appeared, which stopped being true when the loadout customizer landed on the start page. An id pointing at nothing isn't an error in HTML; the box just stops suggesting, silently.

`Ops` draws its own now. One subtlety worth flagging: I made the id **per-editor** (`useId()`) rather than the fixed `controlNames-weapons`, because Settings renders one `Ops` for the terms and another for *every rule* — a shared name would have put the same id on the page a dozen times and bound every field but the first to someone else's list. The obvious fix would have created that bug.

Three tests asserted the literal id; they now assert that a field's `list` resolves to a datalist that exists — the invariant that was actually broken, which the old assertion couldn't see.

Verified in the browser: 13 name fields, **0 orphaned references**, 487 weapons / 116 ashes / 1651 items, and `Ru` matches the same seven your Settings screenshot shows. [PR #280](https://github.com/SCRT-HQ/runlog/pull/280).

## Great Runes

The data has a wrinkle: **each rune exists twice** — the one a boss drops and the one a Divine Tower gives back. Only the restored form does anything, and the ids/events run in a neat block (`0x400000BF`–`0xC4` / events 191–196, plus the Unborn at 197).

`GiveGreatRunes` hands over all seven restored, item and event together. Plus **ten Rune Arcs by name**, since a great rune does nothing until an arc is spent. [PR #281](https://github.com/SCRT-HQ/runlog/pull/281).

Two notes:

- `HotkeyActions.GreatRunes` already existed and is a red herring — it opens the *restoration menu*, the screen you use at a tower while already holding an unrestored rune. It grants nothing.
- **Miquella's Great Rune** and the **Phantom Great Rune** are giveable by name *today* — they're the only two runes with no event behind them. Left out because neither is a main-boss drop, but either is one line if you want it.

**Unverified in-game.** The open question is whether the restored item plus its flag is enough, or whether the game also wants the flag for the unrestored one it replaces. Both the setup and the fork commit say so.

content.text:
I had the pouches backwards, and your "no error either" is what exposed it.

## The mistake

I read your event-log capture as *cause* when it was *record*. `60500`/`60510`/`60520` fired **as the pouches arrived** — they're the game's note that it already handed one over. Writing the note hands nothing over. And spawning the item can't work either: all three share one item id and hold one, which is what made this look impossible at first.

The award is the operation. Each pouch has an item lot:

```
10000    Stormveil, Margit
10050    Enia, for two great runes
101100   Finger Reader Enia, Godfrey
```

`AwardItemsIncludingClients` runs the game's own routine, which grants the slot *and* writes the flag itself. `GiveStartingFlasks` was already doing exactly this — `AwardItemsIncludingClients(2000)` — and I didn't look at it closely enough before writing the flag version.

Fixed on `integration` as `45b8866`.

**This casts doubt on two others I wrote the same way.** `GiveStartingGifts` and `GiveGreatRunes` both spawn-item-plus-set-flag. That's right where the item is the thing you use (a whistle, a rune you equip) and the flag only prevents re-award — but if either turns out to do nothing in game, the award-lot route is the fix, and the lots are in the same table.

## Handing out

You're right, and the cause is a deliberate design decision biting. `withChosen` folds the loadout into `profile.setup` client-side — *"one field on the wire, nothing on the server had to learn what a setup is"* — so by the time hand-out calls `setupFor`, terms and loadout are indistinguishable and it sends both.

I've started the fix on `handing-out-is-the-loadout`: `ProfileOp` gains `chosen`, `withChosen` marks the loadout's ops, and `opsOf` carries it across the wire (it currently strips anything but `op`/`args`/`once`). Then hand-out sends only the marked ops while attach still sends everything. Not finished — I'll complete it next unless you'd rather I did something else first.

## Also open

- [#283](https://github.com/SCRT-HQ/runlog/pull/283) collision reporting — verified on Open the Map + Start of the DLC, names all three shared presses.
- The half-finished-row thing was yours, not a bug — though the editor *does* let a required arg stay empty until the tool refuses it. Still happy to surface that earlier if you want.

I've got two of the three pinned down, but not the first — let me not build on a guess.

**On the address hydration, your instinct is exactly right.** `addressFor()` needs a watch key that arrives two ways: `watchKeyHere()` from localStorage, or `reach?.key` from a fetch. Without it the address renders as `REPLACE-WITH-YOUR-WATCH-KEY`. It also needs `run=` and the run to be **open to watchers**, or the tool is refused at the door.

**On not seeing yourself:** the panel renders `run.members`, which is the server's session member list. A solo run that has never been shared has no members, so the list is empty — including you. That's the bug.

**On "Someone has connected a control":** I searched the client and server and that string doesn't exist in either. The nearest things are `Attached` ("*TarnishedTool* is listening…") and a member row falling back to `"Somebody"`. So I'm probably looking at the wrong surface.

Press **Hand it out** and the tool was sent the whole setup: the loadout picked for the run *and* the pack's own terms, the second of which nobody asked to be given again. A pack whose terms hand over starting flasks handed them over on every press, and by the third one it is a different game.

## Why they were one thing

They are one list. `withChosen` folds the run's loadout into `profile.setup` on the way to the snapshot — which is exactly what lets the server know nothing about loadouts — and the server sent that list under the id `setup`.

One effect could not have worked anyway. A tool applying an id it already holds takes the first one off before applying again (`EffectRunner.Run` → `Revert(frame.Id, quiet: true)`), which is right, and it means a press meant to re-send the loadout would have reverted the run's terms and re-applied them with it.

## The split

The fold marks its own lines with `chosen`. The server sends two effects:

```json
{ "t": "apply", "id": "setup",   "label": "The run's terms",   "each": true, "ops": [ … ] }
{ "t": "apply", "id": "loadout", "label": "The run's loadout", "each": true, "ops": [ … ] }
```

Attaching sends both. The button sends `loadout` alone and leaves `setup` where it is.

`tidy` had to learn the field too — it rebuilds every operation from the three fields it knew about on the way to the same snapshot, so without that the marker was written and dropped a line later.

## The record was never written

Separate bug, same complaint, found on the way. `termsGiven` has been on `updateSession`'s patch type since the terms learned to be given once, and the real `updateSession` never put it in the row. The handler tests hand the handlers a `Map`, which stores whatever it is given, so the suite was no evidence at all about the file that talks to DynamoDB.

**On a deployed run, every reconnection was handed the runes again.**

The loadout gets `loadoutGiven` beside it rather than sharing: the terms go out on attach and never again, the loadout goes out on attach *and* whenever the host presses the button, and one field could not answer both questions without lying about one.

`hosted/infra/test/store.test.ts` is new and exists for that class of bug: the store reached directly with the Put inspected, rather than through a fake that agrees with whatever it is told.

Three PRs, two merged, one in the queue.

**Merged**
- **#284** — the People panel now shows you in a solo run, `Attached` names whose game, and every row has a Copy address button. Plus a timeout fix for the `ControlSettings` test CI was failing on: it takes 2s to parse the shipped TarnishedTool profile against a 5s default, which is not a margin.
- **#285** — your `seeded` mode removal from `elden-ring-tarnishedtool.yaml`, 3.3.1 → 3.3.2. I left `seededRuns` in the capability list; nothing sets `seeded: true` now, so say the word if you'd rather it went too.

**#286, rebased and queued** — the hand-out fix you diagnosed, plus a second bug found underneath it.

The loadout and the pack's terms travel as one list (that's what keeps the server ignorant of loadouts) and went out as one `apply` under the id `setup`. One effect could never have worked: `EffectRunner.Run` reverts an id before re-applying it, so pressing **Hand it out** was always going to take the run's terms off and put them back, gifts included. Now the fold marks its lines `chosen`, the server sends `setup` and `loadout` as separate effects, and the button re-sends `loadout` alone.

The second bug: `termsGiven` has been on `updateSession`'s patch type since the terms learned `once`, and the real `updateSession` never wrote it to the row. The handler tests hand the handlers a `Map`, which stores whatever it's given — so the suite said nothing about the file that talks to DynamoDB. **On a deployed run, every reconnection re-gave the runes.** `hosted/infra/test/store.test.ts` is new and inspects the actual Put.

Still open from earlier: whether `GiveStartingGifts` and `GiveGreatRunes` need the award-lot treatment the talisman pouches needed, and `GiveTalismanPouches` doing nothing silently in your last game test.

I removed the Seeded mode since the UI lets you enter a seed regardless of mode, so I didn't see a point. I like that overall design better in general, just default it as an always available option and let the presence of a value determine if it should be seeded or not.
Let me see what `seeded` actually gates today.

content.text:
Makes sense, and the code is most of the way there already — the seed field is shown on every mode. What isn't there is the engine honoring it.

**What I found**

`seededRun` is computed in two places and both want a seed *and* the mode flag:

- `packages/engine/src/drive.ts:237` and `:265`
- `apps/web/src/run/useRun.ts:316`

So on an ordinary mode a seed gets a *different, weaker* stream — `createRandom(\`${seed}:${events.length}\`)`, keyed by how far down the log you are, so one extra event shifts every roll after it — and only when auto-roll is on. A seeded mode gets the addressed stream (unit + purpose + occurrence), which survives two runs diverging. Meanwhile the start page already tells you "With a seed, the rolls the app makes for you come out the same every time it is entered." That promise isn't kept.

**One decision before I touch it.** `mode.seeded` currently means two things at once: rolls are reproducible, *and* the app takes over rolling (`useRun.ts:863` — a seeded run refuses your physical dice, because several people can't meet the same sequence if one is typing in numbers off their desk). Under "the seed decides", entering a seed on a solo mode would silently take your dice away.

I'd keep those separate:

- **the seed** decides how the app draws — present, addressed stream, rolls labeled `seeded`; absent, unrepeatable
- **`mode.seeded`** keeps its other job — "meant to be shared", so the app rolls and your own dice would break it

That matches the copy already on screen ("Your own dice are yours regardless") and leaves `seeded` meaningful for the docs line, the feature tag, and the `seededRuns` lint rule.

**Scope:** drop the mode check in those three spots, delete the `events.length` fallback, and open the race gate (`RunView.tsx:934` is `chosen?.seeded || raceCode`) to any run with a seed — note that #285 just made Elden Ring un-raceable, since its only seeded mode is gone.

One consequence worth naming: an in-flight run that has a seed on a non-seeded mode would draw its *future* rolls from a different stream. Past rolls are already in the log and don't move.

You're right, and the code already says so — I was preserving a distinction its own comment argues against.

Nothing. That's the answer — every behavior `mode.seeded` gates is a consequence of *having a seed*, not of the mode:

- the addressed stream (`useRun.ts:320`) — reproducible because there's a seed
- the app rolling instead of waiting for your dice — and the comment at `useRun.ts:310` already puts this on the seed, not the mode: *"a seed overrides the auto-roll preference rather than sitting alongside it"*
- Draw again being off (`useRun.ts:858`) — *"a skipped draw would put this device's dice out of step with everyone else's"*, which is true the moment a seed exists

My split was wrong. There's no dice-policy job left for the mode flag to hold, and keeping one would mean two people with the same seed getting different runs depending on which mode they picked — which is the bug, not the design.

**Revised, smaller:** the seed decides everything. `mode.seeded` is left with one job — the start page *insists* on a seed instead of offering one ("A shared mode needs one"), so you can't start a shared mode unseeded and wonder why nobody matches you. Plus the non-behavioral uses: the `seeded` feature tag for finding packs meant for shared play, the docs line, and the `seededRuns` capability lint.

Eight packs declare it (demo, forfeits, ladder-work, practice-room, rocket-league-ladder ×2, engine-testing, and your private one); under this they all keep meaning something sensible.

Changes: drop the mode check at `drive.ts:237`, `drive.ts:265`, `useRun.ts:316`; delete the `${seed}:${events.length}` fallback in both; open the race gate at `RunView.tsx:934`. Same caveat as before — an in-flight run with a seed on a non-seeded mode draws future rolls from a different stream; past rolls are in the log and don't move.

input.command:
git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
feat(run): the seed decides whether a run is seeded

A run counted as seeded only where it had a seed *and* its mode declared
itself seeded. So two people who had agreed on a seed met different runs
depending on which mode they picked, and the box they typed it into had
already told them otherwise: "the rolls the app makes for you come out
the same every time it is entered."

They did not. An ordinary mode with a seed took the other branch,
`createRandom(`${seed}:${events.length}`)`, keyed by how far down the log
a roll falls rather than by where in the game it is -- so the two went
out of step the moment one of them logged anything the other did not --
and only when auto-roll happened to be on.

Now the seed is the whole of it, in the driver and in the app both. One
stream, addressed by unit, purpose and occurrence, which is what lets two
runs diverge and still meet the same dungeon. A seed also turns rolling
on, as it always did for a shared mode: a seed does nothing for dice
thrown on a desk, so asking for one is asking the app to roll.

`modes.*.seeded` keeps one job, and it is not about dice: a mode meant to
be shared cannot start without a seed, because starting one unseeded
gives you a private run and no sign that nobody will ever match it. It
still carries the `seeded` feature tag and the `seededRuns` capability
tie for finding packs built for shared play.

Races follow. Starting one wanted a mode declaring itself seeded, which
left a pack whose author had not written one unable to race at all;
`Start a race` is now on every setup screen and mints a seed where the
box was left empty.

One consequence: a run already in flight with a seed on an ordinary mode
draws its future rolls from the addressed stream instead of the old one.
Rolls already in its log do not move.

`randomFor` and `rollingContext` no longer take a `pack`; nothing outside
`drive.ts` called either.
EOF
